commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes Solution Prep's services and gives a phone number for consultations at the end
key_insights: Over 80% of colleges were test-optional at time of filming, but several selective schools and some state systems had reverted to requiring scores for all applicants
Most schools use Score Choice (submit only your best sitting) and many superscore (roughly 90% for SAT, 70% for ACT, per speaker), so check each school's specific policy rather than assuming
Whether the new digital SAT and the old paper SAT can be superscored together is unresolved/school-specific and should be confirmed directly with the college
Some schools accept self-reported scores during application but require an official score report upon enrollment; misreporting can get an acceptance revoked

Key decision heuristic: find the college's 25th-75th percentile SAT/ACT range via its Common Data Set; submit if above the 75th percentile, generally submit if within the range, and generally don't submit if below the 25th percentile (at test-optional schools)
Colleges rarely publish both 'percent who applied without scores' and 'percent who got in without scores,' which would let applicants judge whether omitting scores truly helps

The 25th-75th percentile figure is an aggregate across the whole class (all majors, in-state/out-of-state), so a score 'in range' doesn't guarantee competitiveness for a specific major or as an out-of-state applicant
Dartmouth (when it reinstated testing) said it evaluates scores relative to the applicant's own high school's typical scores, not just against a national bar
specific_numbers_or_facts: Over 80% of colleges test-optional at time of recording; Harvard, Yale, Brown, Dartmouth, Caltech cited as having reverted to requiring scores, along with public systems in Florida, Georgia, Texas, Indiana, Tennessee
~90% of colleges superscore the SAT, ~70% superscore the ACT (per speaker)
Most recent Common Data Set referenced was 2023-24 at time of filming
notable_or_distinctive: Gives a concrete, actionable decision rule (25th/75th percentile via Common Data Set) rather than vague 'it depends' advice, and explicitly flags the unresolved question of digital/paper SAT superscoring.
reliability_notes: Superscoring/test-optional percentages are stated without citation and likely approximate; policy landscape (test-optional vs. required) changes year to year, so specific school examples are time-sensitive and may be outdated by the time this is viewed.
